The split screen takes a little getting used to at first and then you don't even notice it.

Just an absolute joy to play and hands-down the best couch coop game I have played in about two and a half decades of PC gaming (yikes I'm getting old...).

I finished this game with my wife.
Each level is a complete standalone game.

I really feel more connected to my wife after that.
The world needs more of these creative games made with love.

I purchased this game specifically to play with my significant other. While we expected it to be good, It Takes Two, the sophomore effort from developer, Hazelight, impressed us so much, it is now the benchmark for which I will measure future co-op game experiences. We simply lost count of how many charming moments we encountered whilst playing.
I could go on and on, but, the selling points of this game are best experienced for yourself.
Each painstakingly detailed level in this title offers you unique gameplay mechanics that are never recycled. Communication and cooperation are a must, as well as decent twitch response reflexes. Various mini-games are scattered around the environment, and give you a slight reprieve from your main objective, only to get your competitive juices flowing. (sore losers need not apply!) 
Controls are tight and responsive, and the camera does a decent job of keeping track of the action. However, those who suffer from motion sickness may occasionally become disoriented or even nauseated due to the mandatory split screen. 
Overall, this is a very high quality, one of a kind experience that could only be produced as a labor of love. 
Pick this one up, play it with someone special, and let the hilarity ensue.

Highly recommended.

A healthy marriage is like the ultimate co-op game: You have to know when to give and take, when to push and pull, and when to talk and when to listen. But most importantly, you must always remember when it’s your turn to take the garbage out - something Hazelight Studios has certainly done during the development of the almost entirely garbage-free It Takes Two. This utterly superb co-op platformer manages to cram in enough unique and exhilarating gameplay ideas to give Shigeru Miyamoto a migraine, with not a single dud among them.

Centering around a pair of pint-sized parents, May and Cody, It Takes Two is a bit like Honey, I Shrunk the Kids if the director had been tripping on LSD. The world around you isn’t merely supersized, but augmented with all manner of fabulous contraptions and anthropomorphic everything. May and Cody’s journey from their garden shed back to their house takes them on dazzling detours through everywhere from outer space to a tiny nightclub housed inside an air conditioning vent (attended by grooving hordes of anthropomorphic glow sticks, naturally), and serves as a sustained, 10-hour-long blast of co-op platforming bliss that’s constantly conjuring up new ways to engage and entertain.

[h1] 9.5/10 [/h1]

It Takes Two definitely deserves all the awards it has. This is probably the best representative work of the ninth art of the game: game content that can be enjoyed by any age, shocking camera movement and animation, rich and detailed scene design, fine modeling, wonderful music, and philosophical content of the story, and most importantly as a game, it has very creative gameplay and top-level design.

It is generally believed that there is a close connection between this work and A way out. The two games have many similarities in gameplay, but in this one, you can see a leap in game quality. This game is undoubtedly suitable for people of any age, even if they are not very interested in games, they could enjoy it a lot.

This game is simply too good. But in my opinion, the only shortcoming is that the plot is not too impressive-and this may also be a compromise for all ages. The most impressive thing about this game is the ability that coordinate between characters on different levels. I never felt bored and tired throughout the game, and I was always shocked by the creator's creative ideas. And since the game director is also a movie screenwriter, you can enjoy a visual feast that is no less than a Hollywood movie experience.

No matter what kind of gamer you are, this game is definitely worth a try, and it will not let you down. If there are a few shortcomings of this game, apart from the fact that the plot is difficult to impress the players deeply, I am afraid that you must need a friend to play -after all, you can't play a co-op game alone, isn't it?

With approximately 55,000 reviews -- 96% of them positive -- at the time of my posting this, it is hard to know what more I can add to [i]It Take Two[/i]'s well-deserved acclaim.  As others have said, it is an excellent cooperative multiplayer game with very satisfying controls, varied levels, and superb production values in art and audio.

Aside from these things, what stood out to me was the game's decency.  It is *anti*-exploitative, quite deliberately excluding features like collectibles (let alone microtransactions) or character advancement that are predicated on Skinner box treatment of the player.  Rather than finding ways to [i]take[/i] more from the player (money, time, etc.), the developers have found ways to [i]give[/i] more to the player, with many small delights to be found.  In addition to not exploiting the player, the game doesn't exploit its characters -- only very occasionally playing the cheap tropes that the game's set-up would tend to invite.  The game's narrative may lack subtlety and surprise, but its straightforward positive message never feels preachy, perhaps because the scenario is so ridiculous.

It is rare to play a big-budget game (the credits go on FOREVER!) that seems to have as its goal that players will find a fun, full, satisfying experience and go away better than they came.

I was born in '91, and started playing videogames with the Sega Genesis when I was 5 or 6. Ever since, I played hundreds... thousands of games. This game is something else. It's majestic game design. Seriously, no one has ever done a better coop game than this one. The way the story unfolds, the characters, the topics they discuss. Even the message the game sent! It's incredibly well written.
And the most important thing: Game mechanics. The game introduces scenarios and mechanics that quickly get discarded before it turns repetitive. Every new segment of the game is worthy of wonder, both by its visual but also by surprise: they always make you do something different, unique. Something that the game will never let you do again. It's like playing 15 different games under the same premise.

The only aspect you have to consider is that this game is better for couples. Playing it with a friend is fun, but you'll be missing a lot of references to the relationship with your couple.

Do yourself a favor and play this game as soon as you can.

[h1]It Takes Two is game that represents the pinnacle of co-op.[/h1]
It's been a long time since I've played a game like It Takes Two. Very few games are able to truly understand the meaning of a cooperative experience. A lot of games tout "co-op" as a major feature of the game, but it never expands past the fact that you can play the game with your friends. Games like It Takes Two and Portal 2 aren't like that. This game is not functional without a friend and it takes full advantage of that fact. I highly recommend picking this game up especially since your friend can hitch a ride with you for free with the Friend's Pass or Steam Remote Play.

Gameplay has always been the biggest selling point of any video game and It Takes Two does not disappoint. It's a cooperative puzzle platformer at its core, but don't let that brief description fool you. It Takes Two is constantly throwing gameplay elements from every possible genre to keep things fresh for the whole experience. One moment you're playing a third person shooter with an extremely deadly combo attack and the next moment you're playing a top-down RPG with magic spells. Every chapter of the game gives you a new toy to play with and each mechanic is flushed out to its fullest potential. There was one moment when I thought an area's gimmick was fairly boring with the magnets, but then shortly after I was given a turret that fired magnets that were used to traverse a massive wall. The sheer amount of genres displayed here makes It Takes Two look like a love letter to video games as a whole. And that's not even mentioning the fact that each player gets a different toy to play with. The only exception is the magnet level, but every chapter gives both Cody and May a different tool and mechanic to play around with. Let's use the shooter chapter I mentioned earlier as an example: Cody gets a goop gun that stuns enemies and May gets a flare gun that ignites bugs. And that's where the beautiful cooperative elements come into play, combining those two guns together creates a massive explosion that instantly kills most enemies. It Takes Two's fearlessness when it comes to new mechanics and the fact that the two playable characters offer different experiences makes it so this game has amazing replay value. Movement is another thing the game loves to play around with. There are tons of different vehicles for you to operate in drastically different methods. And that's not to say the game is weak without these mechanics, the core platforming and puzzle solving are strong in their own right. Every puzzle felt very natural and my friend and I never once had to look up a guide when we got stumped. Overall, the game design showcased here is an absolute marvel.

Something I wasn't expecting to praise this game for is the artwork and environmental design. While the normal human models are kind of uncanny to look at to me, I think the toy models you actually play as and everything else look really nice! All of the artwork is fairly pretty and what I believe should be the standard for modern AAA games. There's a lot of attention to texture and detail for every model in the game and I really appreciate that. I swear it's good but it's hard to write "This fur looks like actual real-life fur" for too long. What I was really taken aback by was the amount of unique environments that were explored. I was worried that the game was going to entirely take place inside the house and everything was just going to be navigating furniture. That fear was quickly shot away as soon as I started exploring the inside of a tree-cave-like-system and inevitably found my way to a medieval castle. One of my personal favorite environments was the use of a snowy wasteland village that entirely took place inside of a snow-globe. It's a treat that the environments are as varied as the game design. And for a platformer, it's pretty important that the environment you navigate is interesting to look around for where you need to go to next. Oh and a quick note: I recommend turning off the soundtrack and listening to your own music of choice. The soundtrack isn't all that engaging and it's very cliche at some moments.

However, my biggest complaint for It Takes Two has to be the game's story and writing. The plot is simple, Cody and May are getting a divorce and The Book of Love is a magical entity trying to get them to fall back in love. A love story would sort of imply that the main characters would have some actual chemistry, but I didn't believe Cody and May liked each other (even as just friends) for a single moment. It was very weird for them to be constantly at each other's throats and blaming each other for every little thing only for them to get back together seemingly out of nowhere in the final chapter. There was no build-up to that moment. There wasn't a slow second spark of love, they just went a complete 180 on their opinion of each other in the span of a few minutes. There was even a moment where my friend and I mocked Cody for complaining that May isn't at home because she's paying the bills. Cody and May in general aren't very interesting characters anyways, as they boil down to the stay-at-home mom and stay-at-work dad tropes with the genders swapped. Dr. Hakim was also an extremely annoying character that the game wanted me to like, but he only filled the role of an irritating antagonist up until the final chapter. Tone is something I think It Takes Two struggles with. It's a divorce story with profane language, but with such a childish attitude and understanding of the whole situation, so much so that it got to the point that it was actually humorous. There was a major plot point where the couple decided the best course of action was to make their daughter cry and that was eventually followed with one of the darkest scenes I've seen recently. If you've played the game, you know what I'm talking about and it was completely out of nowhere to me. Both my friend and I didn't care for the story at all and we actively wished for a different outcome in regards to the ending. It's really hard to care about a love story when both of the main characters are insufferable and hate each other.

Overall, It Takes Two is worth the $40 price point. It was really surprising to see EA publish a genuinely good game, although that's most likely because they had little involvement in the creative process. It Takes Two is a wonderful experience that I enjoyed from start to finish. There wasn't a single dull moment in the 12 hour playtime. [b]I give this game a solid 8/10 and I'm really hopeful Hazelight is able to make another amazing co-op story adventure in the future. The only thing that's preventing it from being a perfect 10 is its story, I think It Takes Two is that good.[/b]

[h3][i]It Takes Two[/i] | Perfect Game Review [/h3] 
(100% Completion at 11.7 Hours)
[hr][/hr]
[i]It Takes Two[/i] made me realise that sometimes, dragging your romantic partner through chaos is the ultimate relationship test… but I wouldn’t know. I played this game with my gamer best friend instead of my wife, so this was an absolute breeze.

[b]Gameplay:[/b] By constantly reinventing itself with creative mechanics and surprising level design that actually makes you and your partner communicate (or argue), the gameplay in [i]It Takes Two[/i] never got dull during our first playthrough. ★★★★★

[b]Graphics:[/b] With many vibrant and detailed environments to cooperate through, [i]It Takes Two[/i] often feels like jumping into a Pixar film on a sugar high. From flying through the air on fidget spinners in a kid’s bedroom to ice skating across a snow globe, the entire game was a visual delight. ★★★★★

[b]Sound:[/b] Surprisingly dynamic and shifting appropriately with the tone of each level with lively voice acting from the main characters. However, the overall soundtrack was not as memorable to me compared to other aspects of the game. ★★★★☆

[b]Story:[/b] Fluctuates well between funny, heartfelt, and unhinged moments. The core narrative—parents being forced to reconcile their nearly broken marriage while solving puzzles as miniaturised dolls—is earnest, but unrealistic at times. While the story scenes were well presented, I honestly found the script to be a bit cringey. ★★★☆☆

[b]Replayability:[/b] [i]It Takes Two[/i] was a solid one-and-done for me—fun while it lasted, but not something I’d replay unless swapping roles. Also, it would be best if you waited for a sale, since perfecting it in under 15 hours didn’t quite justify paying full price. ★★☆☆☆

[b]Final Thoughts:[/b] [i]It Takes Two[/i] understands that being cooperative isn’t just about playing together—it’s about problem-solving, yelling, laughing, and somehow having a great time through all the chaos. Even if some parts are a bit too quirky for their own good, the creativity and polish make it one of the best couch co-op experiences out there.

[h3]Overall Rating: 8/10, more affordable (and entertaining) than couples counselling.[/h3]

I never write real reviews for games but this honestly the first time I ever really felt compelled to write something that had such an impact on how I view the medium of Cooperative games.

When I first heard of the game I was shocked to realize it was from Josef Fares (A Way Out, The Game Awards “Fuck The Oscars” guy (legend).) I had known him firstly from when Jerma985 played A Way Out on stream with a friend and thought of the concept of how Josef tackled Co-op games was interesting; something that was in real need of innovation because it always just feels like an afterthought with most games. While the way it was tackled was interesting, I thought the gameplay itself was more or less lacking in comparison to the story and ideas that they kept serving up to the two playing. 

Finally It Takes Two was announced and honestly at first I thought it looked corny and such a weird departure from the more serious tone Josef’s game had in the past. I was cautiously optimistic regardless of my really baseless first impression because as we know from Josef, passion and determination run through that man’s blood like water runs through a river. 

After waiting for a while since launch and somewhat keeping an eye on the game, I was shocked to see the sheer amount of positive reviews for the game (and the bad takes from negative reviews from people who played like, 1 hour of the game that took me nearly 15 to finish.) I decided to take a chance on the game, to get myself out of the rut of playing my usual 3-4 games I do. I bought a copy for my best friend and I for their birthday after casually mentioning it here and there. I wasn’t too pleased with Origin integration (side note, fuck game launchers, stop making us launch from 2 separate things!) but I knew it was just a necessary minor inconvenience in order to play.

Let me tell you, the reviews do not lie about how fantastic this game is. From the first moments you can move around you feel how fluid the 3D platforming is, coupled with the beautiful graphics and genuinely fun gameplay. I was actually impressed from the first level of the game. It was such a simple idea turned into this adorable, fun and quirky adventure between this couple trying to fix their broken relationship. The various game elements that shift every chapter to add constant variety without feeling overwhelming having to adapt to how you face new challenges. Level design is so creative and fun that every new area just kept me filled with awe as I constantly wondered how they could possibly top the previous area. I could talk more about the story, gameplay, levels, concepts all day but I would be afraid of spoiler territory for folks who are questioning whether or not to get this. 

It’s hard for me to remember the last time I had my face light up in surprise or like, genuine fun over experiencing a game. The memories you have with the person you play with could go on and on. There are many games that influence this, because in art we’re always informed by the things we’re inspired by; but few actually are able to mold the medium to create something so compelling and fun. It was an experience from front to back that was so much fun and I’m happy I got to experience it with someone. 

Edit: We are now dating

Let me start by saying this: It Takes Two is not just a game. It's a relationship boot camp disguised as a couch co-op masterpiece. It’s therapy, teamwork drills, and absolute chaos wrapped in the most creative storyline I’ve ever seen in a game. If Pixar and your relationship counselor made a baby, this would be it.

Now, I went into this thinking, “How hard could it be?” Turns out... very. There were moments when I was majestically failing at every jump, puzzle, and timing challenge, while my duo (who I’m convinced is part ninja, part Einstein) was flying through it all like a caffeinated squirrel. Of course, fast-forward a few levels, and the tables turned. Suddenly he was the one crashing into walls and dying spectacularly while I was doing aerial stunts like a pro. Balance, I guess.

The game is built for two people, literally. You cannot play solo, and honestly, that’s the charm. You need each other to survive, to progress, and occasionally to scream, “WHAT ARE YOU EVEN DOING?!” It tests your communication skills, your patience, and your ability to not throw your controller when your partner presses the wrong button for the 17th time.

The story? Oh man. Best. Ever. No spoilers here, but imagine a heartfelt, emotional rollercoaster wrapped in hilarious dialogue and breathtakingly unique levels. One moment you’re bouncing on jello, the next you’re fighting squirrels, then suddenly you’re flying a plane made of underpants. It never lets up and never gets boring.

Whether you’re a couple trying to spice up date night, siblings who want to prove who the real favorite is, or best friends who think they’ve seen it all, It Takes Two will challenge you, make you laugh, frustrate you (in the best way), and leave you wanting more.

If you survive it without passive aggressively muting your mic, you know your bond is real.

And hey, if you all like this review, I’ll happily jump into Split Fiction next and share my chaos filled thoughts there too.

Final verdict: 10/10. Would fail epically with my partner again.

[b]It Takes Two – A Game That Earned Every Bit of Its GOTY Crown[/b]

It isn’t just a co-op game. It’s a reminder of why games can be art, why they can surprise you, and why they can make you feel things you didn’t expect — even when you think you’ve seen it all.

I played it with a close male friend, and despite not playing it with a romantic partner, the game still managed to stir emotions in a very real way. That alone says a lot about how strong its storytelling and character work are. The themes of connection, communication, and growth cut through the screen, regardless of who you’re sharing the controller with.

From a pure gameplay perspective, the game is ridiculously creative. Every level introduces new mechanics, ideas, and twists, and none of them overstay their welcome. Just when you think, “Okay, I get this,” the game moves on and reinvents itself again. It feels handcrafted, playful, and confident — like a team that knew exactly what kind of experience they wanted to deliver.

Visually and artistically, it’s bursting with personality. Environments are imaginative, expressive, and constantly surprising. There’s a childlike sense of wonder mixed with emotional maturity, which is a rare balance to pull off this well.

This was also my first Game of the Year winner that I actually played on Steam, and honestly? I get it now. This is what GOTY is supposed to mean — not just technical excellence, but a game that leaves a lasting impression.

Not everything was perfect. Near the very end, we started running into frustrating disconnect issues on my friend’s side. Thankfully, we managed to bypass it by playing locally through Parsec, so it didn’t rob us of the ending — but it’s still worth mentioning.

Even with that hiccup, It Takes Two is unforgettable. It’s bold, emotional, endlessly inventive, and deeply human. Few games make you smile, laugh, feel uncomfortable, and reflect — all while asking you to cooperate and trust the person next to you.

It's hard to describe It Takes Two. On the surface, it looks like a normal third-person platformer and that's what it is for the most part but it definitely isn't all the game is offering.
The game has a great variety of sections. A great selection of sections you can select.
There are chapters where the game plays like a third-person shooter. You and your friend each get a gun with unique abilities that you use to shoot down enemies and get through obstacles. There's also a lot of puzzle-solving, side-scrolling, fighting, racing, all kinds of platforming (they get really creative with platforming sections), and even a "Diablo-like" hack 'n' slash chapter where you and your friend play as a wizard and a knight. In this hack 'n' slash chapter you both have different abilities and the entire chapter is in an isometric view.
There are also a bunch of mini-games to be found. In mini-games, you compete against each other in various challenges such as ice skating, target shooting, snowball fighting, etc.
Mini-games are really fun and a great way to breathe from the oh-so chaotic and over-the-top fast-paced campaign.
I say chaotic and fast-paced and the game is all that but it's also pretty casual and fun so don't be frightened by those scary words. It Takes Two is a great game for both "gaming veterans" and people who are new to gaming.

From time to time you also end up in these big sandbox areas. You can explore around in those areas freely and exploring them is extremely rewarding and satisfying. You can stumble upon easter eggs, secret platforming sections, find previously mentioned mini-games and just discover both cute and funny stuff to interact with. 99% of the achievements are earned by exploring so be aware of that if you care about achievements. Completing the campaign gets you only one achievement out of 20!

What about the story? Is it any good?
The short answer to those questions is YES.
The story is quite simple and pretty straightforward but it's also a pretty good story.
It's funny, heartwarming, and even a bit traumatic at times. Poor Cutie - Those who know, know.

You play as Cody and May. A married couple is about to divorce each other. You both go to take a nap after another one of your married couple's fights and you wake up as dolls.
In order to get back to your real human bodies, you have to reignite the passion for each other, and to do that you have to work together. COLLABORATION is the keyword.

The characters are well written, the humor is top-notch and never feels forced, and overall just great casual and family-friendly fun. It Takes Two is a breath of fresh air in terms of storytelling and combat alike.

Definitely worth the full price not to mention only one person needs to buy the game and your friends can just download the free friend pass to play with you.
There's also split-screen co-op which I used to play this gem of a game with my girlfriend and it was a truly pleasant experience. I know some people think your PC has to run two games at once when playing games in split-screen but that isn't true. Ran perfectly fine in 1440p, everything maxed out at 120fps.

It's a great game to play with your friends but I'd say you definitely should play it with your girlfriend/boyfriend.

You follow the story of Cody and May. They get shrunk down and need to find a way to get back to their normal human size. As you get shrunk down, everyday stuff like a book, a closet or a bed suddenly become huge, and this is where for me personally the magic lies in the story/environments of It Takes Two.

Gameplay feels great. Movement is really well done, interaction with objects is good and during the game you get a wide variety of weapons and abilities. The game mixes combat, platforming, racing and much more really well. And not only mechanics change, perspective also changes. From third person, to 2D, to top-down. Everything is blended together perfectly. Never once during the game I felt like mechanics became boring.

The story of It Takes Two is also really well done. It’s interesting, entertaining, has humor and the further you get, the more you start to actually live with the characters, and understand them.

Environments are definitely the strength of It Takes Two. As I said above you walk around in everyday scenarios such as a garden, a bedroom, a childrens playroom etc. The twist is, because you’re so small all these environments get a complete other dynamic. Suddenly you’re spending tens of minutes just to climb a bed, that small garden with plants becomes its own world where squirrels are bigger than you, you become friends with spiders and that small pond becomes a real challenge to cross. Not only are environments interesting, original and well thought through, they’re also filled with easter eggs, minigames and fun little interactions. I highly recommend taking a minute and exploring every corner of a map. You’ll find so many small interactions and details that make you smile. This has to be one of the most detailed games I’ve ever played.

From the main music, to character voices to small details like walking over a piano and actually hearing each key have its own tone. Props to the developers for the amount of detail.

The absolute mad man that is Josef Farres is back with yet another pure co-op adventure.

Story:

The story of It Takes Two follows on two characters, Cody and May (you pick which one you want to play as in the opening minutes of the game). Their marriage is on the rocks and they are planning on getting a divorce. When your young daughter Rose hears of this, she runs off and begs for her parents to stay together and when she sheds her tears on two dolls, Cody and May consciousness are transported into the dolls. A book Rose owns named Dr. Hakim is your guide into exploring the crazy world around you while you try to save your marriage. 

The story of It Takes Two is absolutely delightful and is filled to the brim with plenty of magical moments and crazy set pieces that just create a one of a kind experience. The writing is top notch and the banter between the two leads is great and hilarious as they bicker constantly. There's plenty of laugh out loud moments as well and with how crazy the story gets at times, you will certainly going to crack up at the antics of the characters. 

Graphics:

Graphically It Takes Two is a really brilliant looking game. You go through plenty of different environments and all of them feel incredibly alive to the point where taking some time off and exploring your surroundings just to take all of it in is just amazing. Going through winter wonderlands, toy sets, outer space and the wilderness is just amazing and some of the environments in the game are absolutely stunning.

The design of Cody and May is also incredibly simplistic yet quite charming. They definitely look like something a kid would make out of spare parts and play with them, with some rough edges on them. Other NPC's you encounter through the game are also really unique and you visit plenty of environments through the game and their inhabitants differ in each location you visit to match the themes of the area, with tons of attention to detail. 

Audio:

The audio design of It Takes Two is also incredibly top notch. The voice acting is incredible across the board and every single actor nails their characters. It's filled to the brim with charm and emotion that makes the experience that much more enjoyable when playing. 

The music is also incredibly charming, from relaxing tracks to awesome intense tracks during the more action packed moments of the game. Not to mention there's an entire chapter themed after music which has some of the best music in the game. 

Gameplay:

Back when A Way Out came out, Josef Farres stated in interviews that the game would never have the same activity twice in a row, so in each level you would always do something new. I was shocked that this statement was true and It Takes Two takes that idea to an even new extreme. 

On the surface level It Takes Two is a 3D Platformer where you and your friend need to work together as a team to make it through the dangerous environments as you try to restore your marriage. You do plenty of jumping on platforms, however each level takes it up a notch and introduces a new gameplay element to keep things fresh from level to level. 

For example in one level the main two characters get two different tools with Cody getting a nail which he throw and make a platform for May to use, while May gets a hammer that allows you to destroy items and allows you to swing on the before mentioned nails. Once the level is done you get an entirely new set of mechanics like weapons, or super powers and that changes gameplay in major ways.

Some of these moments are just purely amazing and you need to see them yourself to actually believe that yes that actually did just happen. Each chapter just gets increasingly more amazing and honestly that's where I will stop as not to spoil the amazing surprises this game has hidden for you to find.

Now to break up the tedium of the story you can find plenty of other thing around the world like spots where you can interact with things like cameras, a painting canvas and a printer, etch a sketch and plenty of other things. One thing that was pretty popular in A Way Out was the competition mini games. Every so often Leo and Vincent will come across a friendly competition to take a break of them escaping from police. Cody and May also find these things scattered around the world. 

There's around 25 mini games you can find throughout the entire game and some of these are just tons of fun. One of these games me and my teammate found ourselves going back to even after finishing the game it was just that much fun and we had tons of fun competing against each other. However a few of these aren't that great, but that's like 2 mini games out of 25.

Verdict:

It Takes Two is pure and simple a borderline masterpiece. It's an amazing game that sparked so much joy and fun that most games wish they could do. If you have a friend or family member to tag along for the ride the experience is one of a kind and I have no trouble recommending it. Apart from minor technical hiccups like frame drops in certain areas, this game is pretty much perfect in my eyes and worth the money. Josef, wherever you take us next in your next crazy adventure, I will be there Day 1. 

Final Rating:
10/10

+ Incredibly charming and funny story
+ Visuals are stunning
+ Great audio design
+ Each level is tons of fun and adds new mechanics to keep things fresh
+ Mini games provide a nice palette cleanser
+ Adding a pro just for that one easter egg

Cons:
N/A

[h3]⚔️ Gameplay & Exploration: [/h3]

It Takes Two is a co-op adventure where players take on the roles of Cody and May, a married couple on the brink of divorce who are magically transformed into dolls. The game requires both players to collaborate to solve puzzles, defeat enemies, and navigate beautifully crafted environments.

The gameplay is incredibly varied, with new mechanics introduced almost every chapter, ranging from platforming to combat, racing, and more. This ensures that the experience feels fresh and exciting throughout its 12-15 hour runtime. Each character has unique abilities that complement the other, fostering a true sense of partnership.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3408741236

[h3]🏆 Completion: [/h3]

To fully complete It Takes Two, players will need to explore every nook and cranny for collectibles and achievements, many of which are tied to optional mini-games and secrets. The best part is that each chapter indicates the mini-games if you missed them and guides can offer support in finding the secrets.

[h3]🏞 Visuals & Presentation: [/h3]

The game’s visuals are a feast for the eyes, with imaginative and detailed environments ranging from a lush garden to a snowy mountain and even a space-themed adventure. The art style is colorful and whimsical, perfectly complementing the game’s tone.

One of the most expansive and well detailed world I've ever encountered, to the point you will easily feel overwhelmed and swept away from actually finding secrets and areas at first you didn't explore.

My only personal problem with the visuals is the dual screen that can rob you from enjoying the game and taking it all in. I wish there was a way to switch between the dual screen and one screen on the fly when needed.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3408740933

[h3]🔊 Sound & Atmosphere: [/h3]

The voice acting and soundtrack are excellent, adding depth to the emotional story. Each area has its own musical theme, enhancing the immersion and highlighting the unique gameplay mechanics of that chapter.

Characters are well voiced and with the comical moments Dr. Hakim, the Book of Love, brings to the table you'll be in for some giggles and laughs.

[h3]📖 Story & Writing: [/h3]

The narrative focuses on themes of love, communication, and understanding, as Cody and May work together to return to their human forms and rediscover their bond. While the resolution might feel predictable, the journey is heartfelt, with plenty of humor and touching moments along the way.

The game offers little time to adjust in a setting as it moves you into another. The story and the chinematics are excellently done and anybody in a relationship can draw some really good life and relationship lessons.

[h2]A Must Play For Couples[/h2]

This game pushes a positive message that I don't think I've seen before in a video game: 
- "Marriages will have problems"
- "It may feel like there are no resolutions, but it IS possible to salvage the marriage"
- "It's not just about you, think about the effects divorce has on the young children" (my favourite one)

It makes for some surprisingly unique and shockingly dark gameplay. We couldn't believe some of the things we saw (Cutie). The absolute horror, dear gawd....we will never forget lol. I haven't played a co-op game this clever since "A Way Out". The mechanics stay fresh as they keep changing, and they are implemented in really fun and imaginative ways. Ways I've never seen before. Sometimes we stopped moving forward just to have fun goofing around and enjoying whatever mechanic was being implemented at the time. There are mini games littered throughout that are all a blast to play (at least once), and they let you take a break from working together for some friendly competition/feud building.

The controls are responsive, and the graphics are pretty damn good especially if you have the hardware for it. We had a lot of laughs with the characters and the writing, and the voice acting was spot on. Everything feels top notch. I do have small gripes though. First is with the audio. It's happened probably 3 or 4 times during our 16hr playthrough. Sometimes the audio would go out and never return, or go out and return when the sequence changed, then go out again when the sequence changed again. The only fix for this was a hard restart. We've also had UE4 crashes, and even a game breaking bug that we fixed by restarting and doing the sequence over like 3 times. While most of the experience was smooth, it DID happen enough to start slightly getting under our skin at certain points.

As a package though I'd still recommend this game to couples or people in long term relationships. It's a great co-op game period, but I think couples will definitely get the most out of it. If your relationship is currently on the rocks due to games like Overcooked, this game will have you sailing off into the sunset again. Best to wait for a sale though as there are indeed a few bugs, and your mileage may vary.
